The city had a department for everything: water, roads, trees, noise. Eventually, after a series of public meetings, it established a Department of Small Disappearances.

Not missing people. Not stolen cars. Those belonged elsewhere.

This department handled the other things.

The word you knew yesterday but couldn’t remember today. The particular smell of your grandmother’s hallway. The conviction, briefly held at seventeen, that you would become a marine biologist. One good glove.

Its office occupied a narrow building between a pharmacy and a shop that had been “Opening Soon” for eleven years.

Inside, a woman named Mara sat behind a wooden desk. There was no computer. Disappearances tended to get worse around computers.

“What have you lost?” she asked each visitor.

Often they started with something easy.

“A recipe.”

“A number.”

“The name of an actor.”

Mara would wait.

Then, sometimes:

“The way my brother and I used to talk.”

Or:

“I used to like mornings.”

She never promised a recovery. That was the first rule.

The second rule was that nothing could be returned exactly as it had been. The lost glove would have a new darn in the thumb. The remembered hallway would include a door the visitor was sure hadn’t been there. A recovered ambition might turn out to be smaller than remembered, but still usable.

One rainy Thursday, a boy arrived carrying an empty jar.

“I’ve lost the sound the house made before my dad moved out.”

Mara took the jar and held it up to the window.

“Leave this with me,” she said.

After he left, she put it on a shelf beside a tin of forgotten birthdays and a cardboard box labelled *Places That Have Become Car Parks*.

She worked on it for several weeks. Once, late in the evening, she caught a little of what he meant: a cough upstairs, a cupboard closing, the television too loud in another room. Then it was gone again.

When the boy returned, Mara gave him back the jar.

“I couldn’t keep it,” she said.

He nodded, looking at the lid.

“But I found this.”

She handed him a small brass key.

“What does it open?”

“The back door, I think. You’ll have to try it.”

He slipped it into his pocket.

Months later, Mara saw him outside the pharmacy with his father. They were arguing about whether they needed an umbrella. The boy said the rain had stopped. His father held out his palm to check.

Mara passed without interrupting.
